scenes.title: A gift meant to grow for 200 years
scenes.purpose: Problem-first hook: Franklin's plan versus what really happened
takeaways: Franklin left 1,000 pounds per city in 1790
He projected about 131,000 pounds after 100 years
Boston's fund held roughly $5 million around 1990

messages.speaker: novice
messages.text: I saved $1,000 at 5% a year. Why would anyone call that exciting?

messages.speaker: mentor
messages.text: In 1790, Benjamin Franklin left 1,000 pounds each to Boston and Philadelphia, to be lent at 5%.

messages.speaker: mentor
messages.text: He projected about 131,000 pounds per city after 100 years. Around 1990, Boston's fund held roughly $5 million.

messages.speaker: mentor
messages.text: His plan rested on one idea: interest that earns interest.

beats.speaker: novice

en.display: Dr. Rivera, I finally saved 1,000 dollars, and my bank pays 5% a year. Honestly, that feels tiny. Why do people get so excited about interest? Is it really worth the wait?

beats.onScreenIntent: Alex's question appears as the first chat bubble

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Let me take you back to 1790. Interest is the price a borrower pays for using someone else's money. Benjamin Franklin knew that well. In his will, he left 1,000 pounds to Boston and another 1,000 to Philadelphia, to be lent to young craftsmen at 5%.

beats.onScreenIntent: Franklin's gift appears as the mentor's reply

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: He calculated that each fund would hold about 131,000 pounds after 100 years. But the real funds fell far short. When they were closed around 1990, Boston's fund held roughly 5 million dollars, and Philadelphia's only about 2 million.

beats.onScreenIntent: The projection and the disappointing reality

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: So was Franklin wrong? His arithmetic was sound. His plan rested on compound interest, which means interest is added to the balance, so the interest itself earns interest. Today you will see how that engine works, and why idle money breaks it.

beats.onScreenIntent: The key idea: interest that earns interest

scenes.title: Why money has a price
scenes.purpose: Lender versus borrower: interest resolves the tension
takeaways: A saver is a lender to the bank
Interest is the price of waiting
The principal is the starting amount

resolution.label: Interest
resolution.text: The price of using someone else's money for a time

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Every loan has two sides pulling against each other. On one side stands the lender, who gives up spending the money today. When you put money in a bank, you are the lender, because the bank borrows your deposit.

beats.onScreenIntent: The lender side lights up

beats.speaker: novice

en.display: And on the other side is the borrower, right? Someone who needs the money now and promises to pay it back later. But why would the lender agree to wait at all?

beats.onScreenIntent: The borrower side lights up

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Because the borrower pays a price for the wait, and that price is interest. The money lent at the start has its own name. It is called the principal, which means the amount you lend or deposit on day one.

beats.onScreenIntent: Interest resolves the tug of war

scenes.title: Four pillars of growing money
scenes.purpose: The part's roadmap: principal, rate, time, interest on interest
takeaways: Principal, rate and time drive interest
The rate is a yearly percentage
Interest on interest is the fourth pillar

cards.title: Interest rate
cards.body: Yearly interest as a percentage of the principal: 5%

cards.title: Time
cards.body: How many years the money stays invested

cards.title: Interest on interest
cards.body: Each year's interest joins the balance

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: To understand Franklin's plan, we need four pillars. The first pillar is the principal, the money you start with. In our example, that is 1,000 dollars sitting in a savings account.

beats.onScreenIntent: Card 1: principal

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: The second pillar is the interest rate. It means the interest for one year, as a percentage of the principal. A rate of 5% per year means 5 dollars of interest for every 100 dollars you lend.

beats.onScreenIntent: Card 2: interest rate

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: The third pillar is time, counted in years. The longer your money stays invested, the more years the rate gets to work. Franklin planned in centuries, not in months, and that choice mattered a lot.

beats.onScreenIntent: Card 3: time

beats.speaker: novice

en.display: And the fourth pillar is the clever one, right? Interest on interest. Each year's interest joins the balance, so next year the rate works on a bigger amount. That sounds small, but I bet it adds up.

beats.onScreenIntent: Card 4: interest on interest

scenes.title: Simple interest: the straight line
scenes.purpose: Define simple interest and its formula
takeaways: Simple interest uses only the original principal
I = P x r x t
$1,000 at 5% for 3 years earns $150

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Let's start with the simplest method, called simple interest. Simple interest means interest paid only on the original principal. The formula is short: I equals P times r times t.

beats.onScreenIntent: The simple interest formula appears

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Here P is the principal in dollars, r is the yearly rate written as a decimal, and t is the time in years. So 5% becomes 0.05. With 1,000 dollars for 3 years, the interest is 1,000 times 0.05 times 3, which is 150 dollars.

beats.onScreenIntent: Each symbol is labelled, then the example

scenes.title: How compound interest grows
takeaways: Interest joins the balance
Each year multiplies the balance by (1 + r)
The curve gets steeper over time

links.text: Interest is added to the balance at year end
Next year's interest is calculated on the larger balance

text.text: Each year multiplies the balance by

links.text: The balance grows faster every year
The gap over simple interest keeps widening

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Now the engine itself. Compound interest means each year's interest is added to the balance. Then next year's interest is calculated on that larger balance. In the book's words, interest starts earning interest.

beats.onScreenIntent: Condition and action links appear

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Follow the chain. Every year the balance is multiplied by the same factor, one plus r. This pattern is called exponential growth, which means each year multiplies the balance by the same factor. The curve keeps getting steeper. And the gap over simple interest keeps widening.

beats.onScreenIntent: Mechanism, result and consequence complete the chain

scenes.title: Worked example: $1,000 at 5% for 3 years
scenes.purpose: Compute the compound balance year by year
takeaways: Compounding earns $7.63 more than simple interest

data.title: Compound interest, added once a year
data.conclusion: Compounding earns $157.63 of interest, $7.63 more than simple interest's $150.

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Let's put real numbers on it. You deposit 1,000 dollars at 5% a year, and the interest is added once a year. After year one, you have 1,000 times 1.05, which is 1,050 dollars.

beats.onScreenIntent: Given values, then year 1

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: In year two, the rate works on 1,050 dollars, not on 1,000. That gives 1,102.50 dollars. In year three, it works on 1,102.50, and you end with 1,157.63 dollars, rounded to the cent.

beats.onScreenIntent: Years 2 and 3, then the result

beats.speaker: novice

en.display: So compound interest earns 157.63 dollars, while simple interest earned 150. The extra 7.63 dollars is interest earned on earlier interest. It looks small now, but that gap grows every single year.

beats.onScreenIntent: The conclusion compares the two methods

scenes.title: The shortcut that is not compounding
scenes.purpose: Common novice trap versus professional reality
takeaways: Yearly interest times years is simple interest
Write 5% as 0.05
Compounding multiplies; it never just adds

left.heading: COMMON NOVICE TRAP
points: One year's interest times the number of years is compound interest

right.heading: PROFESSIONAL REALITY
points: That shortcut is simple interest: it ignores interest on interest

text.text: each year; it never just adds the same amount.

beats.speaker: novice

en.display: Wait, I have a shortcut. I just take one year's interest and multiply it by the number of years. That is compound interest, right? It seems so much faster than going year by year.

beats.onScreenIntent: The trap side appears

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: That is the most common mistake, and it gives you simple interest instead. It ignores interest on interest. A second trap is using the rate as a whole number. Five percent must be written as 0.05 in the formula, never as 5.

beats.onScreenIntent: The reality side and the verdict appear

scenes.title: Thirty years later
scenes.purpose: Predict, then see simple versus compound growth over decades
takeaways: Simple interest grows in a straight line
Compound interest bends upward
Over decades the gap becomes very large

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Before I show the curves, make a guess. Keep the same 1,000 dollars at 5%, but wait 30 years instead of 3. Will the gap between simple and compound interest be a few dollars, or thousands?

beats.onScreenIntent: Empty axes while the learner predicts

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Here is the answer. Simple interest climbs in a straight line to 2,500 dollars. Compound interest bends upward to about 4,322 dollars. Same money, same rate, same years, yet compounding earns well over twice as much interest.

beats.onScreenIntent: Both curves draw, then the 30-year markers

scenes.title: Checking Franklin's plan
scenes.purpose: Guided application of the formula, then its limits
takeaways: Franklin's math holds: about 131,501 pounds after 100 years
Idle money does not compound
The formula assumes a constant rate

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Let's check Franklin's plan together, step by step. Start with 1,000 pounds. Each year multiplies it by 1.05. After 100 years, 1,000 times 1.05 to the power of 100 is about 131,501 pounds. So his projection of 131,000 was sound.

beats.onScreenIntent: Gift and projection counters run up

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: So why did Boston end with only about 5 million dollars? Fewer craftsmen borrowed than expected, some loans were never repaid, and money sometimes sat idle. The formula also assumes the rate never changes. Compounding only works on money that stays invested.

beats.onScreenIntent: The reality counter and the reasons

scenes.purpose: Mentor wisdom tied back to the opening trap
takeaways: The formula was right; idle money was the problem
Only invested money compounds

messages.speaker: novice
messages.text: So Franklin's arithmetic was right, but the money did not stay invested?

messages.speaker: mentor
messages.text: Exactly. Compounding is powerful, but only for money actually invested at the assumed rate, year after year.

messages.speaker: mentor
messages.text: Next chapter: comparing the rates that banks quote.

beats.speaker: novice

en.display: So Franklin's arithmetic was right, but his money did not stay invested? That changes how I see my own savings. Even my small deposit could grow, as long as I leave it alone.

beats.onScreenIntent: Alex connects the lesson to the opening question

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Exactly. In the author's words, compounding is powerful, but only for money that is actually invested at the assumed rate, year after year. Idle money and early withdrawals break the chain, just as they did for Franklin's funds.

beats.onScreenIntent: The mentor's key lesson

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: In the next chapter, you will learn to compare the rates that banks quote, and a quick way to estimate how long money takes to double. Everything there builds on the compound interest you learned today.

data.title: Simple and compound interest in 8 rules

rules.title: Interest is a price
rules.text: Interest is the price a borrower pays for using someone else's money.

rules.title: Principal
rules.text: The principal is the amount you lend or deposit at the start.

rules.title: Rate as a decimal
rules.text: Write the yearly rate as a decimal: 5% becomes 0.05.

rules.title: Simple interest
rules.text: Simple interest is paid only on the principal: I = P × r × t.

rules.title: Compound interest
rules.text: Compounding adds each year's interest to the balance, so interest earns interest.

rules.title: Multiply by (1 + r)
rules.text: Each year multiplies a compound balance by the same factor, 1 + r.

rules.title: Time matters
rules.text: Over a few years the methods look similar; over decades the gap becomes very large.

rules.title: Only invested money compounds
rules.text: Compounding works only for money actually invested at the assumed rate, year after year.

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Let's gather what we learned into eight rules you can carry with you. Each rule comes straight from Franklin's story and our worked example. Keep them close for the next chapter.

beats.onScreenIntent: The rule thread appears

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Rule 1: interest is the price a borrower pays for using someone else's money. Rule 2: the principal is the amount you lend or deposit at the start, like our 1,000 dollars.

beats.onScreenIntent: Rules 1 and 2

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Rule 3: always write the yearly rate as a decimal, so 5% becomes 0.05. Rule 4: simple interest is paid only on the principal, using I equals P times r times t.

beats.onScreenIntent: Rules 3 and 4

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Rule 5: compounding adds each year's interest to the balance, so interest earns interest. Rule 6: every year, a compound balance is multiplied by the same factor, one plus r.

beats.onScreenIntent: Rules 5 and 6

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Rule 7: over a few years the two methods look similar, but over decades the gap becomes huge. Rule 8, the one Franklin learned the hard way: only money that stays invested keeps compounding.

beats.onScreenIntent: Rules 7 and 8, with rule 8 in the spotlight

beats.speaker: mentor

en.display: Here are all eight rules together. Pause the video and read them once more. With these eight ideas, you are ready to compare the rates that banks advertise in the next chapter.

beats.onScreenIntent: Compact two-column overview of all 8 rules
